title: Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

title: Unpacking the micro–macro transmission mechanism: how home-country culture selectively shapes cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial internationalization
abstract: Abstract International business accounts treat national culture as a country-level antecedent that shifts average export propensity uniformly, leaving the individual-level mechanisms producing within-country heterogeneity in internationalization intensity unspecified. We address this micro–macro transmission gap using social cognitive theory, examining how individualism versus collectivism and risk avoidance versus tolerance selectively recalibrate three cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial export decisions: perceived self-efficacy, perceived opportunity availability, and fear of failure. Our multilevel analysis of 40,529 observations across 41 countries spanning 2010–2019 reveals divergent rather than uniform moderation: individualism amplifies self-efficacy and opportunity availability beliefs through the social validation pathway, while risk avoidance constrains opportunity availability beliefs and fear of failure through the anticipatory self-regulation and outcome expectancy pathways. Fear of failure’s directional relationship with internationalization is contingent on the expectations of failure costs that the home-country cultural environment establishes through the outcome expectancy pathway, rather than being uniformly inhibitory as prior frameworks assume. These findings advance international business microfoundations theory by specifying the observable transmission pathways through which national cultural dimensions produce heterogeneous export intensity outcomes within the same national context. For policymakers, the findings imply that interventions to strengthen self-efficacy or opportunity awareness work best when calibrated to a country’s cultural profile.

EXPRESS: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
abstract: Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales managers . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an aggregate target ( Aggregate Target Scheme , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each individual territory or salesperson ( Individual Target Scheme , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition improved performance , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the reallocation of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a sales star bias —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased joint fieldwork , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.

title: Do PCAOB Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

Innovation booms, easy financing, and human capital accumulation
The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
abstract: Abstract We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.

title: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power
abstract: Fulfillment by Platform (FBP) models, in which e-commerce platforms offer fulfillment services to sellers, have become widely adopted. Although these fulfillment models provide improved service to customers, they have recently drawn criticism from sellers, who argue that existing FBP cost structures hurt seller competition and negatively impact market dynamics. This paper evaluates the effects of FBP on market dynamics in light of such recent criticisms. We use data from a leading online retailing marketplace to evaluate concerns about competition and estimate the effect of downstream fulfillment on upstream supply echelons. Our analysis demonstrates that while the adoption of fulfillment services offered by platforms improves consumer welfare, it also increases market concentration among sellers in the upstream markets. To identify consumers' demand and merchants' cost structures, we employ a structural empirical model. Our findings reveal that the current cost structures of FBP hurt upstream market competition, as measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman index. Specifically, smaller merchants with lower margins are forced to increase their prices more to remain profitable with FBP, leading to a price disadvantage compared to bigger merchants. We find that bigger merchants' profits increase at the expense of smaller players. Merchant welfare for bigger merchants increases by 4.79%, while it reduces by 0.14% for smaller merchants. These findings can have implications for evolving regulatory policies governing two-sided markets. Given the lack of good quality data on both sides of the market in e-commerce settings, our study provides much-needed empirical evidence of platform interventions on market outcomes.

title: Location-Allocation of Emergency Service Systems in Light Traffic
abstract: Light-Traffic Asymptotics for Emergency Service Planning Timely emergency response depends on where rescue teams are stationed and which areas they serve—decisions that shape response times and uncertainty in each team’s service durations and availability. In “Location-Allocation of Emergency Service Systems in Light Traffic,” Xin Wang, Weiliang Liu, Loon Ching Tang, and Zhisheng Ye use light-traffic asymptotics to explicitly capture these decision-dependent effects in tractable queueing-based location-allocation optimization models. The key innovation is to turn limiting queueing behavior as call arrival rates approach zero into explicit approximations for performance losses associated with calls that have to wait. These approximations connect queueing performance to planning decisions, enabling mixed-integer linear programming formulations with theoretical guarantees on solution quality in the light-traffic regime. In simulations using Singapore lift-trap rescue data, the optimized plans reduced projected annual late rescues by about 70% relative to the existing arrangement.

title: EXPRESS: Design and Pricing of Online Dating Subscriptions
abstract: Online dating is now the most common way for new couples in the U.S. to meet, with more than 30% of Americans having used dating apps and annual industry revenues exceeding three billion dollars. Most dating apps monetize through subscription pricing, offering users fixed periods of app access for recurring fees. However, applying subscription pricing to online dating presents unique challenges. Unlike other digital services, users’ valuations of dating app services typically decline over time as continued participation can be costly in terms of both time and emotional effort, and repeated renewals may signal unsuccessful searches. Further, a dating app's dual objectives of (i) building a large user base of paying subscribers, and (ii) successfully matching those users, are ostensibly in tension, since users who achieve their goal of finding a partner subsequently exit the platform. Given the inherently transient nature of user engagement with dating apps, it is notable that leading U.S. dating apps, such as Hinge and Bumble, have begun offering increasingly long subscription options, including lifetime subscriptions. In this paper, we analyze the performance of subscription pricing strategies with varying service lengths for online dating platforms. We propose a natural model of dating app monetization and use it to evaluate how subscription length affects both profit and steady-state user base size. Notably, we find that lifetime subscriptions simultaneously maximize both objectives, providing a compelling explanation for their emerging use. Finally, we extend our analysis to subscription menus with two options and show that offering one short-term option and one lifetime option guarantees at least 57.7% of the optimal performance.

title: EXPRESS: Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment with Timing Coordination Requirements
abstract: We address a tactical planning problem facing organizations that must perform geographically dispersed jobs with timing dependencies using appropriate teams of workers and equipment. This Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment (TWPD) problem, which is motivated by the annual planning and budgeting activity for rail infrastructure maintenance and upgrades, requires making simultaneous decisions on resource sizing and selection, resource-to-job assignment, and resource repositioning to complete all jobs while minimizing resource and transportation costs. Key challenges include timing coordination among jobs, varying resource capabilities, and sequence-dependent changeover costs. Prior scheduling and routing models often focus on short-term decisions, assuming a given set of resources, and do not incorporate complex timing coordination requirements. We propose a large-scale optimization model, with strong timing coordination constraints, that integrates all the features of the TWPD problem. To solve this difficult problem, we propose three new families of valid inequalities to further strengthen the model and develop problem reduction procedures as well as an optimization-based multi-stage algorithm to identify good initial feasible solutions. Our Composite method applies these acceleration strategies before initiating an exact branch-and-bound solution procedure. To test the effectiveness of this method, we first apply it to real data sets for track maintenance from a leading railroad company and compare its performance with a method that uses a standard solver without our enhancements. We find that our method dramatically outperforms the standard method. We also test our method on many randomly generated problems to validate its superior performance and identify problem features that make this problem difficult to solve. When compared to a manual tactical plan, our method quickly generates a near-optimal solution that saves over 15% in annual total cost, demonstrating the practical value and viability of our model and method. We conclude by discussing some managerial implications and insights from our results.

title: EXPRESS: Optimal Return Policies with Heterogeneous Search Rewards
abstract: This paper studies return policy design for an online seller serving consumers who can resolve product-fit uncertainty through costly pre-purchase search, with search rewards varying across consumers. Return policies shape not only post-purchase return behavior but also ex-ante search and purchase decisions, thereby generating endogenous consumer segmentation. One might expect that inexpensive search would reduce the seller's incentive to offer a generous refund. In our baseline model, however, we show that full refund outperforms no refund when search costs are sufficiently low. We trace this result to a fundamental trade-off in implementing a full-refund policy: the search-relief effect versus the return-inducing effect. Full refund substitutes for search by allowing consumers who would otherwise search to purchase directly and evaluate fit after purchase, thereby removing their search-based information advantage and restoring the seller's pricing power. However, it also induces returns from consumers who would otherwise purchase without search and keep the product, sacrificing the revenue generated by their tolerance for misfit. When search costs are sufficiently low, most consumers would otherwise search, and the search-relief effect therefore dominates the return-inducing effect. As search costs fall further, full refund can also achieve a win-win outcome, indicating that pre-purchase search may be socially inefficient. These findings explain when and why sellers may optimally discourage ex-ante search in favor of ex-post product evaluation.

title: What Interruptions Say About Your Organizational Culture
abstract: Recent research suggests that interruptions when meeting attendees are speaking are significant moments that affect how employees experience workplace culture and can lead to self-censoring. Taking a different approach to meeting facilitation can help leaders become more aware of when this is occurring so that they can improve participant dynamics, encourage meeting attendees to contribute, and more effectively respond to interruptions.

title: “The Minimum Wage Is the Maximum Wage”: How Goal Replacement Perpetuates Means–Ends Decoupling
abstract: This research examines how organizations contribute to the perpetuation of means–ends decoupling (MED) within issue-based fields organized around societal problems, under conditions of heightened field scrutiny. In such settings, organizations often profess commitment to field goals and visibly comply with institutionally prescribed practices to satisfy monitoring, reporting, and public evaluation requirements. However, many adopted goals remain underachieved, raising questions about how compliance without progress endures and how claims of commitment remain credible under transparency regimes intended to spur substantive goal pursuit. Our data came from 75 interviews with 68 brands, suppliers, and third-party organizations pursuing worker well-being in global fashion supply chains. We unveil auditability-based goal replacement as an organizational-level mechanism through which actors rhetorically foreground compliance as public evidence of commitment while narrowing internal goal pursuit to auditable thresholds that serve their core goals, thereby allowing shortfalls to persist. Self-silencing about this substitution and the instrumentalizing of shortfalls close the configuration into a self-reinforcing loop. The study advances MED scholarship by (i) showing how organizations leverage field conditions and appropriate the existing scrutiny infrastructures to advance their core goals while reproducing the means–ends gap, (ii) problematizing the authenticity of commitment claims, and (iii) explaining how goal-ineffective compliance prevails as a credible substitute for adopted goals. It also extends research on organizational responses to institutional complexity and calls for greater attention to institutional impact—that is, the realized advancement of the societal aim an institution emerged to address.

title: The Efficiency Trap of Agentic AI in Human Resource Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Agentic AI transforms HRM from data‐driven support to autonomous execution. Organizations deploy these recursive workflows to eliminate human implementation variance, yet we challenge the assumption that such alignment remains optimal. Drawing on Weick's theory of loose coupling, we argue that delegating HR execution to agentic AI creates algorithmic tight coupling. While this generates immediate hyper‐fit, the removal of strategic slack leads to structural calcification, compromising organizational resilience during polycrises. Human line managers provide a critical buffer, enabling the sensemaking necessary to absorb systemic shocks. In contrast, agentic AI workflows governed by instrumental rationality lack the value rationality required for complex organizing. We propose a governance framework to reconcile machine‐driven consistency with the human stewardship required to preserve long‐term organizational adaptability.

title: Designing fulfilling and productive workdays: Effects of task meaningfulness sequences on daily engagement and performance.
abstract: Given the importance of experiencing fulfilling and productive workdays, scholars have focused on ways to boost employees' daily engagement and performance, suggesting this may be accomplished by increasing meaningfulness of their work tasks. However, an alternative approach may be needed in multifaceted work contexts where employees need to complete sets of varied tasks each day, including tasks that lack meaningfulness. To address this issue, we integrate the workday design perspective with research on residual engagement to examine implications of strategically sequencing tasks in terms of their meaningfulness. We theorize that because of a process we refer to as engagement cascade, performing the day's most highly meaningful tasks earlier and in a concentrated manner will tend to produce higher levels of daily engagement relative to sequences in which the most highly meaningful tasks occur later or are disbursed. We use agent-based modeling to formalize the engagement cascade process and generate specific predictions regarding how daily engagement is impacted by different task meaningfulness sequences. Findings from an intensive longitudinal design study with National Aeronautics and Space Administration and Russian Space Agency crew members (Study 1), an experience sampling field experiment with full-time employees (Study 2), and two controlled laboratory experiments with undergraduates (Study 3 and Supplement to Study 3) provide support for our hypotheses. Specifically, the decreasing task meaningfulness sequence engendered higher levels of daily engagement and, in turn, daily performance, relative to the increasing, inverted U-shaped, and U-shaped sequences. title: Common ownership and consumer welfare
abstract: Abstract Rival firms with shared institutional investors (i.e., common owners) may compete less aggressively, potentially harming consumer welfare. Yet, research on common ownership has primarily focused on firm performance, often overlooking welfare outcomes or revealing contradictory results. This paper adopts a strategic network perspective to examine how common ownership affects firms’ service quality and pricing levels, which directly impact consumer welfare, and how customer and competitor factors that alter the focus of competitive strategy moderate these effects. To test the hypotheses, the authors analyze a rich, multi-market dataset of U.S. airline firms from 1995 to 2025. Findings reveal that competing firms with higher common ownership tend to have lower service quality and set higher prices. However, this effect is attenuated for firms with high customer-asset value and amplified among rivals competing across multiple markets. The findings demonstrate common ownership’s influence on firms’ marketing mix strategies and offer actionable insights for managers, policymakers, and investors.

Synthesizing Information-Driven Insider Trade Signals
abstract: Abstract We propose a novel approach to synthesize presumably information-driven insider trading signals for the cross section of stocks. We find that the resulting straightforward composite strategy can often forecast returns in a global sample. This predictability is strongest in equal-weighted portfolios, short holding periods, and insider-buying signals, and it improves further with global diversification. Cross-country analysis reveals that varying insider trading restrictions between countries have limited explanatory power for the performance of the composite strategy. Overall, the results are consistent with a short-term informational advantage of insiders, which might be due to the skillful interpretation of non-private news.

title: Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting
abstract: How Demand Allocation Shapes Inventory Decisions Online platforms that fulfill orders for independent sellers often bear inventory costs without choosing how much sellers stock. In the paper “Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting,” Yilun Chen and Jiaqi Lu study how reallocating customer demand among substitutable products can influence sellers’ inventory decisions. The platform commits to a demand-shifting rule that effectively alters the demand distribution perceived by the sellers. Its optimal rule reduces demand fluctuations around a target inventory level, making that level attractive to sellers and pooling demand risk across them. The authors characterize this rule in closed form. When shifting demand is inexpensive, the platform can achieve the profit available under centralized inventory control, whereas sellers and customers also benefit. However, when shifting is costly and inventory is expensive for the platform, its optimal intervention can reduce customer service levels. The findings show why platforms should assess how demand allocation changes stocking incentives and customer outcomes.

title: Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms
abstract: On the Power of Adaptivity in Choice-Based Matching Platforms Online labor, lodging, and carpooling platforms decide not only whom users can choose but also when those options are shown. Simultaneity can crowd attention around a few popular users and leave many good matches unrealized. In the forthcoming Operations Research paper, “Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms,” the authors study how much platforms gain by updating assortments after observing earlier choices. They compare four policy classes, ranging from showing all assortments at once to fully adaptive policies that process users one by one. They prove that adaptivity within one side improves performance by at most a factor of [Formula: see text], whereas fully adaptive policies improve on one-sided adaptive policies by at most a factor of two; both bounds are tight. They also develop efficient approximation algorithms, extend their results to constrained settings, and empirically show that their methods perform far better than their worst-case guarantees.

title: Hybrid Kidney Allocation: Improving Equity by Fair Integration of Deceased Donor-Initiated Chains in Kidney Exchange
abstract: Problem definition: Living donor kidney exchange programs (KEPs) expand access to transplants by enabling exchanges among patient-donor pairs. However, highly sensitized patients are disproportionately hard to match and face long waits. Deceased donor–initiated chains (DDICs) have been proposed to enable more transplants by diverting an occasional deceased donor kidney from the waitlist to start a KEP chain, which ends by returning a kidney to the waitlist. Yet, DDICs have seen virtually no implementation. In the U.S., this is largely due to concerns that the kidneys returned may differ in blood-type distribution from those diverted, disadvantaging waitlist patients of certain blood types. We study how DDICs can be integrated into KEPs while explicitly protecting blood-type-specific waitlist access. Methodology/results: We develop two forward-looking optimization approaches: one that solves a stochastic model using Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and one that solves a static model with forward-looking constraints. Through simulation, we show that forward-looking models are needed to preserve the blood-type distribution of donations to the waitlist. Under both models, even limited use of DDICs significantly increases transplant rates for highly sensitized patients. While the static approach requires only modest extensions to models as currently used in practice, the more complex and time consuming SAA-based approach yields larger equity gains. Managerial implications: DDICs can improve access to life-saving transplants for the most disadvantaged KEP patients without reducing access for any blood type on the waitlist. By explicitly controlling the blood-type distribution of waitlist donations, matching policies can address objections that have hindered DDIC adoption, calling for renewed policy evaluation.
